panels.rationale: Single lateral radiograph of the left elbow from a case of Coccidioides infection. The caption states 'Left elbow X-ray on admission' and the in-text explicitly attributes the imaging to 'bilateral osteomyelitis of both olecranon (Figures 3 and 4)', with Coccidioides immitis confirmed by culture of incision and drainage and positive coccidioidal serology. The radiograph visibly shows irregularity and destructive change at the olecranon consistent with osteomyelitis, matching the vocabulary entry for coccidioidal osteomyelitis / punched-out osteolytic lesions. Skeletal (osseous) involvement is a recognized but less common disseminated form, hence variant. No ethnicity or age is stated; the panel is bone-only so skin tone is null. panels.rationale: The supplied image is a single axial post-contrast T1-weighted MRI (the panel labeled '(a)' in the source caption) from a biopsy-proven case of disseminated coccidioidomycosis to the spine. It shows T6 vertebral body and paraspinal soft-tissue enhancement with spinal canal compression, corresponding to coccidioidal osteomyelitis/discitis (supported by the article title 'Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis to the Spine' and the in-text biopsy confirmation). It is a real human-patient image of the target disease, so it is included. The source caption additionally references a sagittal MRI (b) and an H&E histology panel (c), but those panels are not present in the provided image, so only this visible axial MRI is classified here as a single-image figure. No skin is shown; age and ethnicity are not stated; no image annotations are present. [raw subtype: disseminated coccidioidomycosis with spinal (vertebral) osteomyelitis]
panels.attribution_text: Ramanathan et al. Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis to the Spine-Case Series and Review of Literature.. Brain sciences 2019. doi:10.3390/brainsci9070160. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Axial T1-weighted magnetic resonance (MR) images with contrast showing extensive vertebral body and soft tissue enhancement with compression of the spinal canal at T6. (b) Sagittal T1-weighted MR Images with contrast showing extensive enhancement throughout the vertebral bodies and soft tissue but most significantly at T6–7. (c) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of the thoracic bone specimen showing acute osteomyelitis with abundant coccidioides organisms. Multinucleated giant cells with engulfed coccidioides spherules is a characteristic finding. Abundant acute inflammatory changes was noted in the marrow cavity.
in_text_mentions: osis. A CT scan of the chest revealed lucencies throughout mid-thoracic spine with adjacent prominence of paraspinal soft tissues suggestive of osteomyelitis and discitis. MRI of the T spine revealed abnormal marrow enhancement seen with varying degrees of paraspinal soft tissue enhancement, the most significant being at T6 where diffuse marrow enhancement and vertebral height loss was seen (Figure 1a,b). A biopsy of the lesion confirmed the coccidioidomycosis (Figure 1c). He was initiated on antifungal therapy—voriconazole and amphotericin B—followed by surgical debridement and stabilization.

in_text_mentions: A 41-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented to the hospital with three days of abdominal pain and a non-healing right calcaneal ulcer. MRI of the right ankle revealed acute osteomyelitis of the posterior calcaneus positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Coccidioides. CT of the abdomen (Figures 1, 2) and subsequent omental biopsy (Figures 3, 4) at the time revealed granulomatous inflammation and coccidioidal peritonitis without malignancy, leading to a diagnosis of disseminated coccidioidomycosis.

B: Right panel is a PAS-stained photomicrograph (400×) of the same patient's skin biopsy showing a Coccidioides spherule, matching the in-text report of Coccidioides spherules on PAS with positive cultures in a disseminated coccidioidomycosis case. ous lesion on the right arm showed granulomatous dermatitis with verrucous and pseudoepitheliomatous squamous proliferation; a periodic acid-Schiff stain revealed Coccidioides spherules (Figure 5 and Figure 6). in_text_mentions: /pleural specimen from thoracotomy showed extensive necrotizing granulomas associated with reactive fibrosis involving both the lung parenchyma and pleura (Figure 3). In addition to the granulomas, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stains revealed numerous large round-to-oval spherules (Figure 4) associated with multinucleate giant cells. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Grocott’s methenamine silver stain (GMS) further highlighted the spherules filled with endospores, which were diagnostic of coccidioidomycosis (Figures 5, 6). Fungal culture of the lung specimen subsequently grew Coccidioides immitis.

Acid-Fast Bacillus stain was negative.

in_text_mentions: lli smears, fungal culture and cytology were all negative. panels.body_site: brain (meninges, basal cisterns, posterior fossa, sulcal subarachnoid spaces)
panels.rationale: Single axial post-contrast T1-weighted brain MRI from a real patient in an article about coccidioidomycosis co-infection. The image and caption show diffuse sulcal, basal cistern and posterior fossa subarachnoid space enhancement, i.e., basilar leptomeningeal enhancement consistent with meningitis, a well-recognized classic manifestation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. Prior caption triage flagged it as a real patient radiology image with no third-party restriction. Attributed to coccidioidomycosis (basilar meningitis enhancement) rather than CMV because the dominant captioned manifestation (basilar meningeal enhancement/meningitis) is the textbook coccidioidal finding and coccidioidomycosis is the primary disease of the article; no subtype is directly supported by the caption.

panels.body_site: larynx (right true vocal fold, right arytenoid, false vocal fold, laryngeal surface of epiglottis)
panels.rationale: Single flexible laryngoscopy image from a real patient in a coccidioidomycosis case report. The view shows right-sided laryngeal pathology: erythematous, edematous tissue with white patches involving the right true vocal fold, right arytenoid cartilage, false vocal fold, and laryngeal surface of the epiglottis. The caption explicitly links these mucosal abnormalities to biopsy-proven Coccidioides spherules, establishing laryngeal coccidioidomycosis. This is a genuine patient endoscopic image of a specific clinical manifestation (laryngeal involvement) of the configured target disease, biopsy-confirmed, so it is included. The spherules key is supported by the caption's biopsy statement; the visible laryngeal mucosal findings (erythema, edema, white patches) are absent from the vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings. Laryngeal involvement is an uncommon/disseminated-site presentation, hence variant typicality. No ethnicity or age is stated; no skin is shown; R/L orientation markers are present.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic images of the final biopsy. (a) Low power magnification shows a background of cicatricial fibrosis with a supervening, nodular, granulomatous, and lymphocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis. (b) This higher power image demonstrates the composition of the infiltrate, with many eosinophils, lymphocytes, and epithelioid granulomas (H and E, 200x). (c) A large fungal spore compatible with a mother sporangium is visible within the cytoplasm of a giant cell (H and E, 1000x). (d) PAS staining highlights fungal elements: Two large mother sporangia (fungal spherules) are visible in the center of the granuloma (PASD, 1000x).
in_text_mentions: inical appearance of the lesions (raised, arciform borders with central clearing) raised suspicion for granuloma annulare. Although histologic findings (poorly formed granulomas accompanied by lymphocytes and eosinophils) were inconsistent with this diagnosis, an off‐label trial of upadacitinib was begun. However, he discontinued this treatment after 3 weeks due to worsening skin involvement and pruritus. Given the treatment‐resistant behavior of the rash, another set of two biopsies was performed 8 months after the patient’s initial presentation, which revealed the findings shown in Figure 2.

Both biopsies showed a florid, benign, eosinophil‐enriched lymphocytic and granulomatous infiltrate (Figure 2(a)) in a background of cicatricial fibrosis compatible with antecedent trauma. The granulomas were cohesive, predominated by epithelioid histiocytes with a few admixed Langhans giant cells and exhibited central fibrinoid degeneration (Figure 2(b)). Some of the granuloma had large, centrally disposed fungal spores in the 20‐micron range (Figure 2(c)); these fungal elements were further highlighted by PAS staining (Figure 2(d)). Although no molecular testing or fungal culture was perform

the eosinophil‐mediated host response may play a role in limiting the coccidioidal disease progression. Thus, the combination of florid eosinophilia, an epithelioid granulomatous response, and large fungal spherules was determined to be most consistent with coccidioidomycosis. No chest X‐ray or coccidioidomycosis serologies were performed; however, given that this patient was otherwise asymptomatic and the pathology indicated a background of cicatricial fibrosis (Figure 2(a)), primary cutaneous coccidioidomycosis secondary to fungal inoculation at a site of trauma was the most likely etiology.

A: Real patient chest radiograph from a case of disseminated coccidioidomycosis; caption and in-text explicitly tie the diffuse bilateral nodular lung lesions to Coccidioides infection (Figure, panel A). The discrete nodular lesions correspond to coccidioidal nodules/granulomas (coccidioidal nodule / fungal granuloma synonyms of the coccidioidoma finding). Diffuse nodular pulmonary infiltrates are a classic radiographic presentation of pulmonary coccidioidomycosis. [raw subtype: disseminated] B: Follow-up chest radiograph of the same patient (dated 2 months later) showing coalescence of the nodular shadows with near-complete white-out of both lung fields; caption and in-text attribute this rapid progression to worsening disseminated coccidioidomycosis with ARDS. Chest radiograph showed diffuse nodular lung lesions bilaterally (Figure, panel A). His leukocyte count was 16.65 x 109/L (neutrophils 85.6%, lymphocytes 6.2%), and C-reactive protein was 21.5 mg/dL (reference value, <0.8 mg/dL). After the patient was admitted, fever persisted and respiratory distress worsened rapidly. He developed severe headache, seizures, and loss of consciousness. He was transferred to the intensive care unit for aggressive management of acute respiratory distress syndrome and deterioration of renal function. Chest radiograph showed coalescence of nodular shadows and almost complete white-out of bilateral lung fields (Figure, panel B). Meropenem, antituberculosis agents, and intravenous voriconazole, 200 mg every 12 hours, were administered.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). B: Grocott's methenamine silver stain of the same chest wall mass biopsy highlighting spherical fungal structures (red arrow) consistent with Coccidioides organisms; caption and in-text confirm fungal organisms in granulomatous inflammation in a case of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. Real human-patient histology with disease-specific finding.

in_text_mentions: In December 2020, a core needle biopsy of the right chest wall mass was performed. The patient developed a right chest wall cellulitis post-biopsy which was treated and resolved with Doxycycline. The pathological examination found no evidence of malignant cells but revealed granulomatous inflammation with necrosis and rare spherical structures highlighted by Grocott's Methenamine Silver stain suggestive of fungal organisms (Figures 3A,B).

plate_findings.evidence: Periodic acid–Schiff staining demonstrating a coccidioidal spherule containing endospores within a granuloma (caption); in-text: PAS-positive spherules containing endospores confirming cutaneous coccidioidomycosis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power (×2) H&E of the punch biopsy from a left glabella pustule in the confirmed cutaneous coccidioidomycosis case that clinically mimicked rosacea; shows granulomatous inflammation, part of the diagnostic histopathologic picture per caption and in-text. B: Medium-power (×20) H&E showing granulomatous mixed inflammatory infiltrate from the patient's glabella biopsy; attributed to cutaneous coccidioidomycosis (biopsy-confirmed) that mimicked rosacea clinically. C: High-power (×40) H&E showing granulomatous inflammation with lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils; histopathologic evidence from the confirmed cutaneous coccidioidomycosis case mimicking rosacea. D: PAS stain at ×40 showing a thick-walled coccidioidal spherule containing endospores within a granuloma—pathognomonic histologic feature of coccidioidomycosis; disease attribution is definitive despite the rosacea-mimicking clinical presentation.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic findings in case of cutaneous coccidioidomycosis mimicking rosacea in immunosuppressed patient, Arizona, USA, 2024. A–C) Granulomatous inflammation with mixed infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils. Hematoxylin and eosin stain; original magnifications ×2 (A), ×20 (B), and ×40 (C). D) Periodic acid–Schiff staining demonstrating a coccidioidal spherule containing endospores within a granuloma. Original magnification ×40.
in_text_mentions: onths after initial symptoms), we performed a punch biopsy of a representative pustule on the left glabella. Histopathology demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils, plus periodic acid–Schiff–positive spherules containing endospores (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of cutaneous coccidioidomycosis. Serologic testing yielded negative IgM and indeterminate IgG results. However, additional confirmatory tests (tissue culture and PCR) were deemed unnecessary given the patient’s residence in an endemic region and characteristic histopathologic findings.

in_text_mentions: Histopathology of the shave biopsy of the lesion revealed several scattered granulomas in the dermis. These included lymphocytes, histiocytes, and endospore-containing spherules, some of which are seen within the giant cells that phagocytosed them (Figure 2). Polarizing microscopy was negative for birefringence. Special stains (Figure 3) with Periodic Acid Schiff (PAS) stain confirmed the presence of Coccidioidomycosis. Acid-Fast Bacillus stain was negative.

in_text_mentions: A 41-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented to the hospital with three days of abdominal pain and a non-healing right calcaneal ulcer. MRI of the right ankle revealed acute osteomyelitis of the posterior calcaneus positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and Coccidioides. CT of the abdomen (Figures 1, 2) and subsequent omental biopsy (Figures 3, 4) at the time revealed granulomatous inflammation and coccidioidal peritonitis without malignancy, leading to a diagnosis of disseminated coccidioidomycosis.

panels.rationale: Single-panel PAS-stained histopathology image from a real patient pleural specimen showing multiple large round thick-walled spherules containing endospores, explicitly captioned and described in-text as diagnostic of coccidioidomycosis. Black arrows annotate the spherules. This is the textbook diagnostic histologic presentation of Coccidioides.

in_text_mentions: /pleural specimen from thoracotomy showed extensive necrotizing granulomas associated with reactive fibrosis involving both the lung parenchyma and pleura (Figure 3). In addition to the granulomas, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stains revealed numerous large round-to-oval spherules (Figure 4) associated with multinucleate giant cells. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Grocott’s methenamine silver stain (GMS) further highlighted the spherules filled with endospores, which were diagnostic of coccidioidomycosis (Figures 5, 6). Fungal culture of the lung specimen subsequently grew Coccidioides immitis.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel (X40) from a human lung biopsy in an educational coccidioidomycosis case. The image shows three ruptured spherules with lightly basophilic endospores surrounded by hemorrhage and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes and macrophages — the textbook histopathologic presentation of Coccididioides infection. Disease attribution is supported by the article title ('Educational case: Coccidioidomycosis'), the caption, and the prior caption-triage result. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is stated.

There was also an epidural enhancement in the upper cervical region, suggestive of infectious or neoplastic involvement. There was no evidence of spinal cord compression or degenerative changes, and the overall findings favored disseminated infection. CT of the chest without contrast (Figure 5) revealed a pleural-based phlegmon in the left lower lobe with osteomyelitis of the adjacent ninth rib and transverse process of T9.

panels.rationale: Axial turbo T2-weighted pelvic MRI from a case report of disseminated skeletal coccidioidomycosis. It is a real patient image with colored arrows marking bilateral iliac osteolytic lesions (purple), a left iliopsoas abscess (blue), and a posterior subcutaneous abscess (orange), corroborated by the in-text description of CT/MRI correlation. The iliac lytic lesions map directly to the vocabulary finding of punched-out osteolytic bone lesions; the macroscopic psoas and subcutaneous abscesses are not histological microabscesses, so they are recorded as proposed findings. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is provided. [raw subtype: disseminated skeletal]

in_text_mentions: A non-contrast CT of the pelvis (Figure 6) showed lytic lesions in the bilateral ilia and left sacrum with involvement of the sacroiliac joint, an enlargement of the left psoas muscle (likely due to infection), and multiple subcutaneous lesions. No masses were seen in the solid abdominal organs. Subsequent MRI (Figure 7) confirmed the CT findings of left psoas abscess and bilateral iliac lesions, as well as another dorsal subcutaneous abscess.

panels.rationale: Single axial non-contrast pelvic CT from the disseminated skeletal coccidioidomycosis case report, with prior-exam urinary contrast. Caption and in-text confirm a real human patient with bilateral iliac and left sacral destructive osteolytic lesions (osteomyelitis), left iliopsoas enlargement from infection, and subcutaneous infectious lesions. The osteolytic bone lesions directly match the configured finding coccidioidomycosis_punched_out_osteolytic_lesions; the psoas and subcutaneous infectious involvement are proposed findings not present in the vocabulary. No other disease is attributed in the caption; prior triage confirms no third-party copyright.

in_text_mentions: A non-contrast CT of the pelvis (Figure 6) showed lytic lesions in the bilateral ilia and left sacrum with involvement of the sacroiliac joint, an enlargement of the left psoas muscle (likely due to infection), and multiple subcutaneous lesions. Subsequent MRI (Figure 7) confirmed the CT findings of left psoas abscess and bilateral iliac lesions, as well as another dorsal subcutaneous abscess.

in_text_mentions: After stabilization and resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis, the patient was transferred to a medical ward in which he started to spike high-grade fevers and complained of new symptoms of hiccups with progressively worsening abdominal pain localized to the right upper quadrant. Physical examination of the lungs was clear to auscultation, and the abdomen was nontender to palpation. A repeat plain chest roentgenogram demonstrated a lingular patchy alveolar density with a 6.9-mm left pulmonary nodule on a posterior-anterior view (Figure 1A).

, the patient had persistent fevers, a nonproductive cough, and hiccups. An abdominal X-ray was negative for any acute pathology. Due to the inconsistency of patient’s presentation with a normal physical examination, a computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast was obtained and revealed numerous cavitary pulmonary nodules with one large pulmonary nodule in the left upper lobe measuring 2.8 cm (Figure 1B). Furthermore, the abdomen had a mildly distended gallbladder with gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, however, there was no adenopathy or organomegaly (Figure 2).

The caption explicitly describes a 6.52 cm × 4.98 cm cavitary lesion, and the in-text mention confirms chest radiography demonstrated a cavitary lesion (Figure 1). The disease-focused article title together with the captioned cavitary manifestation supports attribution to pulmonary cavitary coccidioidomycosis. The image shows a real patient radiograph with measurement annotations (dotted caliper lines labeled D: 65.2 mm and E: 49.8 mm) in the left lower lung field. in_text_mentions: His laboratory findings revealed a white blood cell count of 13.0 K/μL, and chest radiography demonstrated a 4.4 cm cavitary lesion (Figure 1). Further evaluation via chest CT revealed an air fluid level (Figure 2), left hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral tree-in-bud and nodular opacities. Bronchoscopic evaluation did not reveal bronchial abnormalities, but cultures from lavage grew Haemophilus influenza and Group F Streptococcus. He was diagnosed with a necrotizing pneumonia and discharged with amoxicillin clavulanate after resolution of his fever and leukocytosis.

panels.rationale: Single coronal CT temporal bone image from a real patient. The caption and article title attribute the lesion to Coccidioides (confirmed by operative pathology and cultures), and the image shows an erosive otologic process: polypoid soft tissue in the external auditory canal, near-complete middle-ear opacification, and a small malleolar head erosion marked by the arrow. The malleolar head erosion maps to the vocabulary's coccidioidal osteolytic/osteomyelitis bone lesion; the canal polypoid soft tissue and middle-ear opacification are not in the vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings. No third-party restriction; image is diagnostically clear. [raw subtype: mastoiditis]

in_text_mentions: duled tympanomastoidectomy surgery. Laryngoscopy revealed erythematous, edematous tissue with white patches involving the right true vocal fold, arytenoid, false vocal fold, and laryngeal surface of the epiglottis (Figure 1). panels.rationale: Single coronal CT image from a case report titled 'Cervical, Mediastinal, and Pericardial Disseminated Coccidioidomycosis'. The caption and in-text mentions confirm a real patient with a large left-sided neck abscess extending into the superior mediastinum with mass effect on the internal jugular vein, in the setting of proven coccidioidal infection (pericardial tissue demonstrated coccidioidal spherules in the same patient). Yellow arrows annotate the abscess and its mediastinal extension. The abscess represents suppurative fungal infection, matching the vocabulary finding for suppurative fungal microabscesses; the large CT-visible abscess, mediastinal extension, and jugular mass effect are proposed as additional findings not covered by the vocabulary. Cervical/mediastinal involvement is a recognized but less common (variant) presentation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. No ethnicity or age is stated; no skin is shown. [raw subtype: disseminated]

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of both lower extremities showing bilateral crusted, bullous erythematous plaques on the legs and knees. The article title identifies the eruption as a reactive cutaneous manifestation of coccidioidomycosis, the biopsy of the crusted lesion showed a vesiculated subepidermal layer with histiocytic inflammation, and the chest X-ray plus eosinophilia support systemic coccidioidomycosis. The visible crusted plaques match the vocabulary finding of verrucous crusted cutaneous plaques; the bullous/vesicular component is not in the vocabulary and is proposed. Attribution to coccidioidomycosis is strong and panel-specific. [raw subtype: cutaneous]

in_text_mentions: A 27-year-old Caucasian male presented with rash associated with myalgia and fever for 7 days (Figure 10). Multiple open and intact vesicles associated with erythematous subcutaneous tender nodules on both arms, legs, neck, and forehead were noted. There was clear, serous discharge from the vesicles. Biopsy of the crusted lesion over the left knee revealed vesiculated subepidermal layer with histiocytic inflammation of the dermis (Figure 11). Laboratory examination showed WBC count of 11.7 × 103/µL with an AEC of 1200 cells/µL. The chest X-ray showed right upper lobe inflammatory infiltration.

panels.rationale: Single axial chest CT of a human patient showing a large cavitary lesion with air-fluid level in the left lower lobe superior segment (measured 55.9 mm on image). The disease-focused article title ('Spontaneous Pulmonary Rupture of Cavitary Coccidioidomycosis') together with the captioned cavitary lesion supports attribution to cavitary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis; the cavity matches the vocabulary finding coccidioidomycosis_pulmonary_coccidioidal_cavity. The air-fluid level is a less common feature, so typicality is variant. In-text notes a necrotizing pneumonia diagnosis, introducing some attribution uncertainty, but the title and prior triage support coccidioidomycosis. [raw subtype: pulmonary cavitary]

in_text_mentions: His laboratory findings revealed a white blood cell count of 13.0 K/μL, and chest radiography demonstrated a 4.4 cm cavitary lesion (Figure 1). Further evaluation via chest CT revealed an air fluid level (Figure 2), left hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral tree-in-bud and nodular opacities. Bronchoscopic evaluation did not reveal bronchial abnormalities, but cultures from lavage grew Haemophilus influenza and Group F Streptococcus. He was diagnosed with a necrotizing pneumonia and discharged with amoxicillin clavulanate after resolution of his fever and leukocytosis.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel at 20X from a skin biopsy of the left forearm in a patient with coccidioidomycosis (reactive ID-IgM/IgG) and a vesiculobullous rash; the article title attributes the eruption (erythema Sweetobullosum) to coccidioidomycosis. The image shows granulomatous inflammatory cells (labeled GIN) in the dermis with neutrophils and histiocytes, consistent with a coccidioidal reactive cutaneous manifestation. No spherules are described, so the neutrophilic/suppurative histology finding is used and granulomatous dermatitis is proposed.

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology from the fatal coccidioidomycosis autopsy case, showing brain parenchyma with edema and a blood vessel densely packed with inflammatory cells (perivascular inflammatory infiltrate). The caption explicitly notes absence of spherules, so the diagnostic spherule finding cannot be tagged; the suppurative-appearing perivascular inflammatory cell collection is tagged visually as suppurative fungal microabscesses. CNS involvement in this autopsy case with multi-organ disease (lung, liver, brain) represents disseminated coccidioidomycosis; the absence of spherules makes this a variant rather than classic histologic presentation. Real patient image, no third-party restriction, no annotations visible.

panels.rationale: Axial T2 brain MRI from a case report of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. Caption and in-text describe a 4-mm enhancing focus around the right caudate nucleus (septic emboli) and an ulcerative necrotic lesion eroding the right occipital calvaria with epidural extension, consistent with hematogenous dissemination and coccidioidal osteomyelitis. The article title and triage confirm coccidioidomycosis attribution. The calvarial erosion matches the punched-out osteolytic lesion vocabulary entry; the cerebral septic emboli are not in the vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings. [raw subtype: disseminated]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Direct microscopic examination of skin scrapings from a human patient with cutaneous coccidioidomycosis showing a large thick-walled Coccidioidal spherule on 10% KOH preparation at ×1,000 — a classic diagnostic finding of Coccidioides infection. [raw subtype: cutaneous] B: Calcofluor white stain of skin scrapings at ×400 showing fluorescent fungal hyphae, attributed to coccidioidomycosis by the caption and in-text. Hyphae are a recognized but less common microscopic finding in cutaneous coccidioidomycosis compared to the classic spherule form. [raw subtype: cutaneous]

A: Coronal CT of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and spine showing lytic lesions in the iliac and sacroiliac regions in a patient with coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever). Punched-out osteolytic bone lesions are a recognized manifestation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. Arrow annotation points to the right iliac lesion. The diffuse soft-tissue and muscle fluid collections are noted as a proposed finding since they are not in the vocabulary. B: Axial CT of the head showing a focal lytic lesion in the right temporal bone with adjacent focal meningeal thickening in a patient with coccidioidomycosis. Skull lytic lesions and basilar meningeal involvement are recognized manifestations of disseminated coccidioidomycosis with CNS spread. Arrow annotation points to the temporal bone lesion. The meningeal thickening is tagged as basilar meningeal enhancement given the skull-base location and the disease context.

panels.rationale: Sagittal T1 MRI of the cervical spine from a human patient with confirmed disseminated musculoskeletal coccidioidomycosis (article title, caption, and in-text all attribute the lesion to Coccidioides). The image visibly shows a C7 epidural abscess/phlegmon with vertebral body and paravertebral soft tissue involvement, indicated by blue arrows. The in-text explicitly documents discitis, osteomyelitis, and an anterior epidural phlegmonous collection with Coccidioides spherules on biopsy and high complement fixation titers. The epidural abscess/phlegmon itself is not in the allowed vocabulary and is recorded as proposed findings. Spinal epidural involvement is a recognized but uncommon (variant) presentation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. No skin is shown, no ethnicity or age is stated. [raw subtype: disseminated musculoskeletal]

panels.figure_caption: Coronal (A) and axial (B) T1-weighted MRI of the pelvis showed a hypointense soft-tissue and marrow-replacing lesion sparing the pelvic and triradiate cartilage (white arrows). Axial diffusion-weighted imaging suggested marked diffusion restriction (white arrow) within adjacent rim-enhancing soft-tissue collections (red arrow), consistent with abscess formation (C). ADC mapping confirms restricted diffusion with low-signal in the respective bone (white arrows) (D). Axial postcontrast T1 fat-suppressed images demonstrate medial and lateral rim-enhancing fluid collections (red arrows) adjacent to the lesion (white arrow), compatible with abscesses, with surrounding inflammatory enhancement (E). Axial T2 (F) imaging characterized extensive marrow, soft-tissue, and fascial edema surrounding the lesion (white arrow) with a focal fluid collection (red arrow) and smaller lateral abscesses (dashed arrows)

in_text_mentions: Initial treatment included IV amphotericin B and oral fluconazole. However, the patient developed acute kidney injury attributed to amphotericin nephrotoxicity. Renal function stabilized with dose reduction and IV fluids. Despite this, repeat MRI four weeks later revealed worsening osteomyelitis at C6-T1 with severe spinal canal stenosis (Figures 2, 3). Therefore, he underwent anterior cervical corpectomy at C7-T1 followed by posterior spinal fusion from C6 to T2 (Figure 4). He was extubated the following day and transferred to the medical floor.

panels.rationale: Sagittal contrast MRI of the lumbar spine from a confirmed case of disseminated coccidioidomycosis (pathology positive for Coccidioides spherules). The image shows L3 compression fracture with vertebral body destruction and ventral epidural enhancement causing mass effect on the thecal sac, consistent with coccidioidal vertebral osteomyelitis and epidural abscess. This is a rare/atypical manifestation of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. The epidural abscess component is not covered by the vocabulary and is listed as a proposed finding. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (1A, 1B, 1C, 1D). 1A: Sagittal post-contrast cervical MRI from a disease-focused case of disseminated coccidioidomycosis presenting as brachial plexopathy; caption documents a large enhancing extradural mass with foraminal extension, a skeletal/epidural manifestation of the target disease in the same patient. 1B: Axial cervical MRI of the same patient; caption shows the extradural mass displacing the cord with osseous remodeling, attributable to the article's disseminated coccidioidomycosis rather than an unrelated mass, given the disease-focused title and panel-specific caption. 1C: Coronal MRI of the right brachial plexus in the case patient; caption describes thickened hyperintense plexus elements representing neuritis, the presenting feature of the rare disseminated coccidioidomycosis case. 1D: MRI shows vertebral body and transverse process signal abnormality labeled bone involvement in the same patient; skeletal/osteomyelitic dissemination is a...

panels.figure_caption: MRI images of cervical spine and right brachial plexus (1A) MRI of the cervical spine - sagittal view of the neck showing large heterogeneous enhancing right-sided extradural mass in the spinal canal extending over a distance of 9 cm and also extending into all right neural foramina from C3-C4 through C7-T1 levels. (1B) MRI of the cervical spine - axial view again showing extradural mass displacing the spinal cord to the left with evidence for osseous remodeling along the mass. (1C) MRI of the right brachial plexus showing thickened and hyperintense trunks, divisions and cords of the right brachial plexus, which probably represent neuritis. (1D) MRI of the right brachial plexus showing abnormal signal in the right transverse processes of C6 and C7 vertebra, and right aspects of C7 and T1 vertebral bodies, consistent with bone involvement.

(1C) MRI of the right brachial plexus showing thickened and hyperintense trunks, divisions and cords of the right brachial plexus, which probably represent neuritis. (1D) MRI of the right brachial plexus showing abnormal signal in the right transverse processes of C6 and C7 vertebra, and right aspects of C7 and T1 vertebral bodies, consistent with bone involvement.

panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the of the brain and cervical spine with and without contrast T1-weighted images in the axial (a, e, f, g), coronal (b, c), and sagittal (h) planes demonstrate scattered foci of abnormal parenchymal enhancement in the right globus pallidus (a: red arrow) and posterolateral putamen (b: red arrow), lateral aspect left uncus/temporal stem (c: red arrow), right occipital cortex (e: red arrow), as well as diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement along the basilar region (e: green arrow), the midbrain (f: green arrow), the cerebellar folia (g: green arrow) and several bilateral cranial nerves (e: blue arrow) and spinal cord (h: green arrow). Multiple subependymal nodules along the lateral ventricles with an increased T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) signal (d: purple arrow).
